Title: Operations/Preservations Control / Environment for the Operation of Processes / Customer & External Provider Property
1. Purpose

To define a system for identifying and planning operations, ensuring they are carried out under controlled conditions.
To establish a system for identification and traceability of materials, products, and documents throughout product realization.
To manage and control customer property.
To determine and manage the work environment needed to achieve conformity to product requirements.
2. Scope

This procedure applies to the Operations PIC (Person-in-Charge), which includes the CEO, Director of Global Operations, Manager, and Consultant.
3. Definitions

This procedure applies to the Operations PIC (Person-in-Charge), which includes the CEO, Director of Global Operations, Manager, and Consultant.
3. Definitions

XTRANET: A network or system that allows controlled access to authorized external customers, suppliers, and other businesses.
WORK ORDER: An internal document used to initiate work, detailing customer name, project description, delivery date, etc.
Project PIC: Person-in-Charge for the Project.
Operations PIC: Person-in-Charge for Operations, as defined in Section 2.
4. Process Description

4.1 Operations Planning & Control:

4.1.1 The Sales PIC receives inquiries, prepares quotations, and obtains customer purchase orders.
4.1.2 All orders, including verbal ones, must be confirmed by a Project PIC.
4.1.3 The Project PIC confirms order acceptance by creating a work order and informing the Operations PIC to kick off the project.
4.1.4 The Operations PIC reviews the work order and assigns the job to an internal/external Project PIC (or Translator, if applicable), confirming the delivery date.
4.1.5 The Project PIC updates the project schedule on XTRANET, outlining tasks, responsibilities, and target completion dates.
4.1.6 The Project PIC ensures the project is completed by the target date, meeting requirements through effective monitoring.
4.1.7 For each project, the Project PIC prepares a Project Task Request form to confirm requirements and monitor progress.
4.1.8 The Project PIC ensures all operational processes are controlled to deliver products and services that meet requirements.

4.1.8 The Project PIC ensures all operational processes are controlled to deliver products and services that meet requirements.
4.1.9 The Project PIC identifies and uses appropriate resources and equipment to ensure service delivery.
4.1.10 The Project PIC establishes and maintains documented information from project design and development, ensuring it covers traceability, verification, validation, and review activities.
4.2 Review of Requirements for Products & Services:

4.2.1 Before committing to provide products/services, the Operations PIC ensures:
Requirements are defined.
Contract/order requirements are different from those previously expressed.
The organization can meet the requirements.
4.2.2 Where customer requirements are not formally documented, the Operations PIC confirms them before acceptance.
4.2.3 If product/service requirements change, the Operations PIC ensures relevant documented information is amended and personnel are aware of the changes.
4.3 Property belonging to customers or external providers:

4.3.1 All customer-provided property (e.g., equipment, documents, intellectual property) for use or incorporation into products/services must be identified, verified, protected, and safeguarded.
4.3.2 Any loss, damage, or unsuitability of customer or external provider property is reported to them and documented.
4.4 Preservation of Conformity:

4.4.1 The Operations PIC preserves the conformity of products and services during processing and delivery to customer requirements.
4.4.2 This includes identification, handling, packaging, storage, transmission/transport, and protection.
4.4.3 Post-delivery activities (e.g., warranty provisions, contractual obligations, recycling) are performed when required.
4.4.4 Control of changes for production and service provision is documented, with review results, actions, and authorizations recorded.
4.4.5 The Operations PIC performs monitoring and measurement at planned stages to verify product and service requirements are met, retaining evidence of conformity and authorization for release.
4.4.6 Nonconforming outputs are identified and controlled to prevent unintended use or delivery, with actions taken based on the nature of the nonconformity.

Title: Monitoring & Measurement of Product
1. Purpose

To define the procedure for the inspection and testing of materials/products to specified product and legal requirements and the necessary controls to achieve and maintain the required standard.
To define a system for the identification of inspection and test status to ensure that only materials/products that have passed the required inspection and test are released/used.
To define a control and review system to prevent the inadvertent use or release of nonconforming materials/products and to reach a consensus on customer requirements for products and services.
2. Scope

This procedure applies to the Project PIC (Person-in-Charge) (i.e., CEO, Director of Global Operations, Manager, and Consultant).
3. Definitions

This procedure applies to the Project PIC (Person-in-Charge) (i.e., CEO, Director of Global Operations, Manager, and Consultant).
3. Definitions

XTRANET: A network or system that allows controlled access to authorized external customers, suppliers, and other businesses.
WORK ORDER: An internal document used to initiate work, detailing customer name, project description, delivery date, etc.
Project PIC: Person-in-Charge for the Project.
Operations PIC: Person-in-Charge for Operations, as defined in Section 2 of QP-OPS-01.
4. Process Description

4.1 Monitoring and Measurement of Product:

4.1 Monitoring and Measurement of Product:

4.1.1 The Project PIC performs monitoring and measurement of product characteristics at appropriate stages of the product realization process, aligning with planned arrangements and the product's Inspection & Test Plan.
4.1.2 This monitoring and measurement activity is carried out to verify that product requirements have been met.
4.1.3 Evidence of conformity with the acceptance criteria is maintained, and records indicate the person(s) authorizing the release of the product for delivery to the customer.
4.1.4 Product release and service delivery to the customer do not proceed until all planned arrangements have been satisfactorily completed, unless otherwise approved by the relevant authority and, where applicable, by the customer.
4.2 Control of Nonconforming Output:

4.2.1 Nonconforming outputs (e.g., products, processes, services) are identified and controlled to prevent their unintended use or delivery.
4.2.2 The Project PIC takes appropriate action based on the nature of the nonconformity and its effect on the conformity of products and services. This applies to nonconforming output at any stage of product realization.
4.2.3 Documented information is maintained for:
The nonconformity.
The actions taken.
Any concessions obtained.
The authority determining action concerning the nonconformity.
4.2.4 When a nonconforming output is corrected, it is subject to re-verification to confirm conformity with requirements.
4.2.5 Nonconforming outputs detected after delivery or during service provision are addressed appropriately.

1. Purpose

To define a system for monitoring customer satisfaction/dissatisfaction for continual improvement and enhancement of customer satisfaction.

This procedure applies to the Sales PIC (Person-in-Charge), which includes the CEO, COO, Manager, and Consultant.
3. Responsibility

-The data collected on customer satisfaction level is analyzed to determine the root cause(s) of any dissatisfaction or problem.

Definitions:

Quality Procedure (QP): A document detailing the purpose and scope of a function and specifying by whom and how it is to be correctly managed.
Controlled Copy: An identifiable copy of the Quality Manual, Quality Procedure or Quality Plan which is distributed, revised or replaced through a written Document Control Procedure which assures that the document reflects all current requirements.

Uncontrolled Copy: An identifiable copy of the Quality Manual, Quality Procedure or Quality Plan which is distributed through a Document Control Procedure, but there is no assurance that later, the document always reflects all current requirements. Just because you can't see the caller, it doesn't mean you have the right to suspend the normal rules of politeness.

Summary
Make messages concise
Email messages are often more difficult to read than other printed matter, and long emails can quickly discourage recipients. Use an easy-to-read layout. Paragraphs should be short, with blank lines between each paragraph. When making separate points, number them or use bullets so they can easily be identified.
Be direct
While personal communications are driven by factors such as appearance and tone, email is based solely on written words. It can be very difficult to determine the sender’s demeanor from the text of an email, and subtleties of tone can easily be misunderstood.
Make your points clearly and directly, and be obvious in your meanings. Remember this when reading email as well – a tone that appears to be aggressive or derogatory may simply be the result of someone’s haste in dashing off a reply. Reread messages to see if you may be misinterpreting the words.
Be Courteous

Be Courteous
Always be courteous and use words like ‘Dear, Nice to hear from you, Thanks a million, Take care’ in your email. Always start your email with Dear / Hi [Person’s name] and thank them for their response, email or enquiry. End off with a short thank you note. As emotions build up in email communication, it is always wise to use the 'right' words in order to receive a positive or respectful response from the other party.
Stick to one topic
Try to avoid covering multiple topics in a single email. When this happens, it is easy for critical information to get overlooked. Instead, cover one matter per email, sending separate messages to cover each unrelated issue, even if the questions or comments are for the same person.
Make the subject meaningful

Make the subject meaningful
Use a subject heading that is meaningful to you and to the recipient. For example, if you’re sending someone product information, write a subject field that has the actual name of the product instead of just “product information.” Similarly, the focus of message thread may change over several email responses. When that occurs, change the message field to reflect the shift – i.e. “Your 10/10 Order (Widget Information)” instead of “Re: Widget Information.”
Keep threads relevant

Keep threads relevant
When responding to emails, use the “reply” button instead of creating a new email so that the previous message is also included. This “message threading” helps ensure that your response can be read in context, and the original sender won’t have to remember the specifics of the original email. But use threads judiciously. Multiple threads can make the email overly long and confuse the reader, especially when the original topic has shifted. Read over old threads and manually remove them when you feel they are no longer appropriate to the topic at hand.
Watch the “cc” field

Watch the “cc” field
Indiscriminate copying of email can clog people’s inboxes, and cause them to habitually ignore messages that really are meant for them. Use the “cc” field only when recipients need to know about a topic. Do not include a list of people in a thread that has become a two-way conversation. In general, use the “to” field to identify the email’s primary recipient/s. Use “cc” for those people who are not active participants, and do not have to reply. Use “bcc” (blind copy) when you want to include a person but don’t want others to know they are receiving it, or when you are sending out to a large group and don’t want to eat up space with several lines of addresses.
Avoid unnecessary attachments

Avoid unnecessary attachments
Large attachments do more than just annoy recipients. They can bring down email boxes (especially those that have an inbox size limitation), and slow down performance. In some cases, delivery of large-sized emails can be delayed by email servers, causing urgent messages to arrive late. Limit attachments only to those that are productive to the recipient, and, when possible, compress files so they take up less space. And be sure to scan all attachments for viruses before you send them – the last thing you want to do is accidentally infect a customer’s network. Large attachments should be uploaded to your personal FTP/WEB account for the other party’s download. (*Anything larger than 5MB)
Use a business tone

Use a business tone
While it is certainly okay to warm up an email with personal greeting and a less-than-formal style, stay away from online slang in business communications. Abbreviations such as LOL (laugh out loud) or BTW (by the way) are best avoided, as are smiley faces :-) and other emoticons. And never, ever, use all uppercase letters -- this is the online equivalent of screaming.
Save “high priority” for the truly urgent
Don’t use your email program’s “high priority” function indiscriminately. Flag emails this way only when you really need to alert the recipient that it requires immediate attention. Show similar caution with the words “urgent” or “important” when used in a message’s subject field.
Proofread before you send

Proofread before you send
Read over every email you create before you send it out to be sure it conveys the message properly. Look at it through the eyes of the recipient to avoid possible misunderstandings or inappropriate comments. Check spelling, grammar, and punctuation; both to make sure they are correct, and that they convey the message properly. If your email program has a spell-check function, as most do, use it.

Following up is an important aspect in client account management and customer service. It helps
